approachQuestion.prompt:
Latest Offer
Each dense ID 0 through n−1 starts with a price. update(id,p) replaces it. cheapest returns the smallest current (price,ID). Every ID always has a current price. Example: initial=[4,7], commands=[update(0,9),cheapest,update(1,2),cheapest] → [(7,1),(2,1)].

2 ≤ n ≤ 100000; n ≤ q ≤ 200000 commands delivered once. Prices fit signed 32 bits. Initial input is read-only. Use ordinary binary heaps without handles or arbitrary-entry deletion; dense ID arrays are allowed. Optimize total command-processing time under this interface. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 100000; n ≤ q ≤ 200000 commands delivered once. Prices fit signed 32 bits. Initial input is read-only. Use ordinary binary heaps without handles or arbitrary-entry deletion; dense ID arrays are allowed. Optimize total command-processing time under this interface.

options.text: Keep current price and version in ID arrays. Each heap entry contains (price,ID,version). On update increment the version and push a new entry. Before cheapest, discard roots with obsolete versions, then return the valid root. Build initial entries bottom-up.
options.feedback: Versions reject obsolete prices without searching the heap. Each obsolete entry is physically discarded at most once, so deletion can be deferred.

options.text: Rebuild a heap from all current prices after each update.
options.feedback: This is correct but repeatedly reconstructs unaffected entries.

options.text: Push new entries but return the root without a version check.
options.feedback: The example returns obsolete (4,0) after update(0,9).

options.text: When an obsolete root is removed, remove every heap entry for that ID as well.
options.feedback: This erases the current offer too. Starting from [1,5], update(0,2) must still permit (2,0) to win.

Versions identify obsolete snapshots even when a price later returns to an earlier value. Purge stale roots before answering cheapest. Old snapshots below the root remain stored, so memory can grow with updates.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A over q≥n commands and n initial IDs. Versions are nonwrapping machine-word counters. Arrays use direct indexing. Heap buffers grow geometrically; charge growth and all stale removals over the entire sequence. No compaction or hashing is performed. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O((n+q) log(n+q+1)) time, O(n+q) auxiliary space
O(q log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(nq log(n+q+1)) time, O(n+q) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Count all inserted snapshots and later removals over the whole command sequence.
details: At most n+q entries are pushed and each is popped at most once. Summing repairs and amortized buffer growth gives O((n+q) log(n+q+1)) total time. Updates without queries can retain all old snapshots, using O(n+q) space. A single query can purge many roots: this is a whole-sequence bound.
“O(q log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Physical stale snapshots can grow with q although logical membership is n.
“O(n+q) time, O(n+q) auxiliary space”: Version checks are constant-time but heap repairs are not.
“O(nq log(n+q+1)) time, O(n+q) auxiliary space”: Entries cannot be purged repeatedly; total purges are bounded by total pushes.
